s: Iphigenia intends to save Pylades by having him carry her tablet to Argos and persuade the king to let him sail safely away. After recognizing Orestes, she realizes that the goal must become their joint return to Argos and urgently searches for a route before the executioners arrive.

l: the recognition of Iphigenia and Orestes, Iphigenia in Tauris, [Enter ORESTES and PYLADES, bound, and guarded by
s: Orestes and Iphigenia recognize one another when Iphigenia dictates a message addressed to Orestes, and Pylades speaks his name. l: Iphigenia's death, Iphigenia in Tauris, [Enter ORESTES and PYLADES, bound, and guarded by
s: Iphigenia's supposed death at Aulis is revealed to have been false because Artemis substituted a fawn and carried her away. In Tauris, she fears that she may instead be forced to participate in Orestes' death.

l: the altar, Iphigenia in Tauris, [Enter ORESTES and PYLADES, bound, and guarded by
s: The altar is the sacred place where the Taurian rite is performed and where Iphigenia says Orestes may be killed. Orestes imagines dying there in his own blood, while Iphigenia remembers that she was once taken to an altar at Aulis.

l: the house of Agamemnon, Iphigenia in Tauris, [Enter ORESTES and PYLADES, bound, and guarded by
s: The house of Agamemnon is portrayed as shipwrecked: Agamemnon is dead, Clytemnestra was killed by Orestes, and Orestes remains afflicted while Electra lives alone. The reunion of Iphigenia and Orestes restores two surviving children of that house to one another, though their danger remains.

l: Iphigenia in Tauris, Iphigenia in Tauris, LEADER.
s: Iphigenia learns that Orestes, pursued by the Furies and suffering from madness, has come with Pylades to take the image of Artemis to Greece as Apollo commanded. l: Pylades, Iphigenia in Tauris, LEADER.
s: Pylades urges Orestes to forget everything but Freedom and warns him not to lose their opportunity. He is identified as the son of King Strophios, Electra's husband, Orestes' cousin and closest friend, and a companion in the planned escape.

l: Orestes, Iphigenia in Tauris, LEADER.
s: Orestes tells Iphigenia that Apollo sent him to the Taurian citadel to seize the image of Artemis and establish it on Attic soil. He recounts his trial at Athens, where Pallas's vote freed him from death, though some of the Furies continued to pursue him. He refuses to abandon Iphigenia and joins the plan to escape with her and the image.

l: Iphigenia, Iphigenia in Tauris, LEADER.
s: Iphigenia recognizes Orestes as her brother and learns that Electra is alive and married to Pylades. She devises a deception in which Orestes and Pylades, guilty of killing their mother, and the image are taken to the sea for purification. She persuades King Thoas to permit the rite and leads the procession out of the temple.

l: Thoas, Iphigenia in Tauris, LEADER.
s: King Thoas questions Iphigenia about removing the image and accepts her claim that the strangers and the image have been defiled. He orders bonds, dark coverings, guards, a citywide prohibition on movement, and the cleansing of the shrine while Iphigenia conducts the supposed purification.

l: Women of the Chorus, Iphigenia in Tauris, LEADER.
s: The Greek women listen to Iphigenia's plea and promise before Zeus that they will keep her secret. They are therefore committed to helping Iphigenia, Orestes, and Pylades escape.

l: the Furies, Iphigenia in Tauris, LEADER.
s: The Furies pursue Orestes because of the bloodshed in his family. Some accept the judgment at Athens and settle beneath that place, but others continue to cling to him like bloodhounds.

l: Artemis, Iphigenia in Tauris, LEADER.
s: Artemis is the goddess whose image Apollo commands Orestes to take from the Taurian citadel to Greece. Iphigenia invokes Artemis's mercy and claims that the image has been defiled and must be purified.

l: Apollo, Iphigenia in Tauris, LEADER.
s: Apollo directs Orestes to seek the Taurian citadel and carry the image of Artemis to Attic soil as the means of gaining freedom. Iphigenia relies on this command as proof that the escape is divinely intended.

l: Argos, Iphigenia in Tauris, LEADER.
s: Argos is Orestes' homeland and the place to which Iphigenia hopes to return. Orestes says that their uncle rules there while he lives in exile, and he promises to carry Iphigenia home across the sea.

l: Greece, Iphigenia in Tauris, LEADER.
s: Greece is the destination of Orestes, Pylades, Iphigenia, and the image. Orestes seeks to take Artemis's image there, while the Greek women long for return to Greek places and Iphigenia hopes to regain her home.

l: the Taurian citadel, Iphigenia in Tauris, LEADER.
s: The Taurian citadel is the place where Apollo commands Orestes to obtain the image of Artemis. It contains the temple and the image from which Iphigenia leads the escape.

l: the sea, Iphigenia in Tauris, LEADER.
s: The sea is presented as the place where impurity can be washed away. Iphigenia uses that belief to persuade Thoas that the strangers and the image must be carried to a secluded channel near the ship.

l: the temple, Iphigenia in Tauris, LEADER.
s: The temple houses the image of Artemis and serves as the setting for the supposed purification. Thoas remains there to purge it with fire while Iphigenia leads the bound strangers and the image toward the sea.

l: image of Artemis, Iphigenia in Tauris, LEADER.
s: The image of Artemis is the object Orestes must take to Greece in order to gain freedom. Iphigenia carries it from its shrine, claiming that it has been defiled by contact with the guilty strangers and must be purified.

l: the ship, Iphigenia in Tauris, LEADER.
s: The ship lies moored near the channel where Iphigenia proposes to conduct the purification. Orestes says that fifty oars are waiting, making it possible for the group to flee by sea.

l: Freedom, Iphigenia in Tauris, LEADER.
s: Freedom is the urgent aim that Pylades tells Orestes to keep in mind. Apollo's command promises Orestes freedom if he takes the image to Greece.

l: Orestes' madness, Iphigenia in Tauris, LEADER.
s: Orestes's madness began after the bloodshed he refuses to name and led him through exile and suffering. Although judgment at Athens freed him from death, some of the Furies still pursue him, and he hopes that completing Apollo's command will end his madness.

l: killing of Clytemnestra by Orestes, Iphigenia in Tauris, LEADER.
s: Orestes says that he and Pylades are guilty of having slain their mother. Iphigenia uses this bloodguilt as the basis for declaring them unclean and requiring their purification before the goddess.

l: Iphigenia and Orestes's escape, Iphigenia in Tauris, LEADER.
s: The escape to Greece depends on secretly taking the image of Artemis to the ship while King Thoas believes that a purification is being performed. Iphigenia, Orestes, Pylades, and the Greek women all contribute to the plan.

l: the purification ritual, Iphigenia in Tauris, LEADER.
s: Iphigenia invents a purification ritual for Orestes, Pylades, and the image, claiming that their bloodguilt has defiled the goddess. She tells Thoas that the rite must occur at the sea and asks him to keep the city still and the shrine under cleansing fire.

l: the planned theft of Artemis' image, Iphigenia in Tauris, LEADER.
s: The planned theft of the image is Apollo's prescribed means of freeing Orestes. Iphigenia carries out the deception by removing the image herself, since no man may touch it, and presenting its removal as part of a sacred purification.

l: the blood sacrifice, Iphigenia in Tauris, LEADER.
s: The blood sacrifice is the customary fate awaiting strangers at the Taurian temple. Iphigenia prevents the immediate sacrifice by claiming that Orestes and Pylades are too polluted to be slain before they and the image have been cleansed.

l: Iphigenia in Tauris, Iphigenia in Tauris, CHORUS. [STROPHE.]
s: The Messenger reports to Thoas that Iphigenia deceived the Tauric guards, freed Orestes, and carried the image of Artemis onto a Greek ship. Thoas orders pursuit, but Athena appears and commands him to stop, declaring that Orestes must take Iphigenia and the image to Greece. Athena assigns the image a temple at Halae, Iphigenia a sacred office at Brauron, and prescribes a blood rite in memory of the old religion. Thoas accepts Athena’s command, frees the women, and allows the Greeks to depart.

l: Artemis, Iphigenia in Tauris, CHORUS. [STROPHE.]
s: Artemis is represented by the heaven-sent image stolen from Tauris. Athena declares that the image will be taken to Greece and honored as Artemis the Tauropole at Halae.

l: Athena, Iphigenia in Tauris, CHORUS. [STROPHE.]
s: Athena appears in a blasting light and commands Thoas to stop pursuing Orestes and Iphigenia. l: Agamemnon, Iphigenia in Tauris, CHORUS. [STROPHE.]
s: Agamemnon is mentioned as the father of Orestes and Iphigenia. The Messenger says that Iphigenia’s escape was accomplished through a plot associated with Agamemnon’s child.

l: Thoas, Iphigenia in Tauris, CHORUS. [STROPHE.]
s: Thoas learns that Iphigenia and Orestes have escaped with the image of Artemis and orders men and boats to pursue them. After Athena intervenes, he submits to her command, releases the women, stops his galleys, and wishes Orestes and Iphigenia well.

l: Iphigenia, Iphigenia in Tauris, CHORUS. [STROPHE.]
s: Iphigenia uses a false cleansing ritual to get the guards away from Orestes, then frees him and carries the image of Artemis onto the Greek ship. Athena orders her to serve at the stair of Brauron, where she will live and die and receive burial.

l: Orestes, Iphigenia in Tauris, CHORUS. [STROPHE.]
s: Orestes is revealed as Agamemnon’s son and Iphigenia’s brother, and he escapes Tauris with her and the image of Artemis. Athena protects him from Thoas, commands him to take the image to Greece, and recalls that she once saved him when the votes of life and death were equal.

l: messenger, Iphigenia in Tauris, CHORUS. [STROPHE.]
s: The Messenger tells Thoas that the strangers have escaped and that Iphigenia stole the image of Artemis. He recounts the false cleansing, the fight at the shore, the ship’s struggle against the sea, and his return to summon Thoas.

l: Women of the Chorus, Iphigenia in Tauris, CHORUS. [STROPHE.]
s: The women of the chorus are accused by Thoas of knowing the plot, but Athena later declares that they are faithful and orders that they be allowed to depart peacefully. They praise the escape and obey Athena’s command.

l: Greeks, Iphigenia in Tauris, CHORUS. [STROPHE.]
s: The Greeks on the ship fight the Tauric men, free Orestes and Iphigenia, and row toward Greece with the image of Artemis. Their ship is driven back toward the rocks by a squall until Athena intervenes.

l: Tauris, Iphigenia in Tauris, CHORUS. [STROPHE.]
s: Tauris is the land from which Orestes, Iphigenia, and the image of Artemis escape. Its ruler Thoas initially sends men to capture them but accepts Athena’s decision that they must leave.

l: Greece, Iphigenia in Tauris, CHORUS. [STROPHE.]
s: Greece is the destination to which Orestes, Iphigenia, and the image of Artemis are sent. Athena orders that the image be established there and that the freed women return to their homes in Greece.

l: Athens, Iphigenia in Tauris, CHORUS. [STROPHE.]

l: image of Artemis, Iphigenia in Tauris, CHORUS. [STROPHE.]
s: Iphigenia steals the image of Artemis during the false cleansing and carries it aboard the Greek ship. Athena commands that it be taken to Greece and installed at Halae, where its history will be remembered.

l: the ship, Iphigenia in Tauris, CHORUS. [STROPHE.]

l: temple at Halae, Iphigenia in Tauris, CHORUS. [STROPHE.]

l: law of mercy, Iphigenia in Tauris, CHORUS. [STROPHE.]

s: Iphigenia’s false cleansing enables her and Orestes to reach the Greek ship with the image of Artemis. Their escape is nearly stopped by the Tauric forces and the storm, but Athena intervenes and secures their departure.

l: the purification ritual, Iphigenia in Tauris, CHORUS. [STROPHE.]
s: The cleansing ritual is a deception devised by Iphigenia. She makes ritual sounds and sings as though she is cleansing Orestes’ blood, while using the guards’ distance to prepare the escape.

l: The Electra of Euripides
s: The document introduces Euripides’ Electra as a realistic, tightly constructed, intellectually rebellious tragedy that revises the Orestes-and-Electra legend associated with Aeschylus and Sophocles. Its central concern is the moral horror of matricide and Apollo’s command, while Electra is presented as the chief figure: damaged by grief, hatred, poverty, frustrated ambition, lost youth, and love for Agamemnon. Living in a poor mountain hut near Argos, she suffers under Clytemnestra and Aegisthus and is married to an honorable Peasant. Orestes returns secretly from exile with Pylades, initially conceals his identity, and is recognized by the Old Man through a childhood scar. The siblings plan revenge: Orestes goes to kill Aegisthus at a feast, while Electra lures Clytemnestra by falsely claiming to have borne a son. A messenger announces Aegisthus’s death, and Electra celebrates over his body. When Clytemnestra arrives, Orestes hesitates, fearing the sin, but Electra presses him onward. They kill their mother in repayment for Agamemnon’s murder and Iphigenia’s sacrifice, then are overwhelmed by guilt. Castor and Polydeuces assign their futures: Electra will marry Pylades, and Orestes will face trial, exile, and eventual release; Apollo’s command is blamed for the deed.

l: Agamemnon, The Electra of Euripides
s: Agamemnon is a king of Argos, chosen by Hellas as chief beyond other kings, and the father of Electra, Orestes, and Iphigenia. He leads the Greek hosts against Troy and returns victorious. At Aulis he kills Iphigenia as a sacrifice, and he later brings another woman into his house. After returning from Troy, Clytemnestra kills him with Aegisthus's involvement. His grave is neglected and dishonored, while Electra and Orestes mourn him and make avenging his murder their central purpose, ultimately killing their mother and Aegisthus.

l: Orestes, The Electra of Euripides
s: Orestes is the exiled son of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra, brother of Electra, friend and ally of Pylades, and a prince without a kingdom. Young, vulnerable to overpowering impulses and will-less brooding, he is raised on hopes of restoration and revenge. Commanded by Apollo and confirmed by an oracle to avenge Agamemnon, he returns secretly from exile to Argos after cleansing and visiting his father’s grave. Concealing his identity at first, he learns of Electra’s suffering and joins her resolve against Aegisthus and Clytemnestra. Recognized by the Old Man, he learns Aegisthus is at a sacrificial feast, goes there with Pylades, and kills him. Though he fears matricide, impurity, and banishment from human sight, Electra presses him to kill Clytemnestra as well. Afterward he is overwhelmed by remorse and fear of blood-guilt. Castor orders him from Argos to seek Athena’s protection in Athens and undergo trial at Ares’ Hill; he must endure exile and pursuit by Keres before promised freedom.

l: Electra, The Electra of Euripides
s: Electra is a woman, daughter of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra, sister of the exiled Orestes, wife of the Peasant yet still a virgin, and the central figure of a tragedy. Childhood suffering leaves her consumed by love for her dead father and brother and hatred for her mother and Aegisthus. Though born to luxury and state, she lives impoverished in a desolate mountain hut, mourning Agamemnon, doing household labor, and grieving her lost youth and status. She longs for Orestes’ return and seeks blood vengeance, ready to use a sword and declaring that she would help kill Clytemnestra with the axe used against Agamemnon. When Orestes returns and is recognized, she devises a summons for Clytemnestra by claiming to have given birth to a son. After Orestes kills Aegisthus, Electra crowns him and Pylades and condemns Aegisthus’s body. She confronts Clytemnestra with accusations, urges Orestes to kill her, gives the signal and word, and assists in the murder. Afterwards, she accepts blame and mourns her mother. By divine decree she is promised to Pylades and must leave Argos.

l: Clytemnestra, The Electra of Euripides
s: Clytemnestra is queen of Argos and Mycenae, first Agamemnon’s wife and later his widow, and mother of Electra, Orestes, and Iphigenia. She is also Castor’s and Polydeuces’ twin sister and becomes Aegisthus’ wife. With Aegisthus, she murders Agamemnon. She defends the killing by citing Agamemnon’s sacrifice of Iphigenia, his bringing another woman into their house, and his exclusion of her from his love. Electra, whom Clytemnestra has allowed to suffer hardship and whom she values less than Aegisthus, lures her to the house by reporting a child’s birth. Clytemnestra arrives to perform rites, asks for mercy by invoking her motherhood, and is killed by Orestes with Electra’s assistance in revenge for Agamemnon’s murder.

l: Aegisthus, The Electra of Euripides
s: Aegisthus is the usurping ruler of Argos and Mycenae and Clytemnestra’s husband and chosen partner after Agamemnon’s death. With her, he plots and benefits from Agamemnon’s murder, then rules harshly: he persecutes Electra, restricts her marriage to prevent an avenger, and mocks Agamemnon’s grave. He fears Orestes, travels guarded, and is encountered outside the city while sacrificing a wreathed ox to the wild-wood nymphs. Believing Orestes and Pylades are travelers, he welcomes them and examines ominous signs. Orestes kills him with a sword, driving him into the house for an ignominious death; he dies alongside Clytemnestra and is to be buried by the people of Argos in a high green grave.

l: Aeschylus, The Electra of Euripides
s: faces matricide [as a horror and a moral problem] Aeschylus faces the horror of the mother-murder rather than avoiding or disguising it. He presents it as both a sin requiring profound suffering and a duty that must be committed because it is commanded by a god.

l: Sophocles, The Electra of Euripides
s: Sophocles deliberately seeks an archaic Homeric style, reacting against Euripides through more classical convention and heroic spirits while avoiding matricide’s dark implications.

l: Apollo, The Electra of Euripides
s: Apollo is a god whose oracle commands Orestes and Electra to avenge Agamemnon by shedding their mother’s blood. The command drives Orestes toward a troubled, miscalled duty; called darkness rather than light, it leaves Apollo bearing the blood-guilt’s stain during Orestes’ trial.

l: the planned matricide, The Electra of Euripides
s: The planned matricide is Orestes' proposed killing of Clytemnestra, Agamemnon's murderer. It is the story's central moral horror: a sin even if commanded by a god, yet treated by Aeschylus as a duty restoring Agamemnon. Orestes fears the oracle's charge while Electra urges the killing; Euripides condemns it and emphasizes its destructive aftermath.

l: revenge, The Electra of Euripides
s: Revenge drives Orestes and Electra to kill Clytemnestra and Aegisthus in response to Agamemnon's murder. The introduction associates revenge with an old savage doctrine that pressures Orestes toward a deed later understood as horrifying.

l: the command to avenge Agamemnon, The Electra of Euripides
s: drives Orestes [towards a miscalled duty] The command to avenge Agamemnon is attributed to Apollo and confirmed for Orestes by an oracle. It creates the conflict between religious duty and the moral horror of murdering one's mother.

l: classicist conventionalism, The Electra of Euripides
s: Classicist conventionalism is represented by standards under which Schlegel judged Euripides' Electra severely. The play is described as a conscious protest against those standards, while Sophocles' treatment is presented as more compatible with them.

l: religious and moral judgment, The Electra of Euripides
s: Religious and moral judgment is central to the contrast among Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides. Aeschylus confronts the conflict between divine command and moral guilt, Sophocles largely avoids it, and Euripides rejects the idea that a god's command can make the evil act right.

l: the Peasant, The Electra of Euripides
s: Electra’s poor but honorable husband is a farmer in a humble mountain dwelling; he protects her virginity, welcomes Orestes and Pylades generously, and is judged to have a prince’s grace.

l: Pylades, The Electra of Euripides
s: Pylades is Orestes’ loyal friend and battle ally. He accompanies Orestes’ secret return to Argos, brings armed servants, helps conceal his identity, assists in killing Aegisthus, and is honored as a partner in victory. Castor then commands him to marry Electra, leave Argos, and establish Orestes’ house on Phocis’ shore.

l: Castor, The Electra of Euripides
s: Castor, a god and Clytemnestra’s maternal brother, appears with Polydeuces after murders, judges her death righteous, directs Orestes and Electra’s futures, and attributes bloodshed to Apollo and fate.

l: Polydeuces, The Electra of Euripides
s: Polydeuces, a god and Clytemnestra’s maternal brother, appears with Castor as a divine Horseman, reveals murder’s consequences, promises Orestes protection, and guards holy, truthful strivers.

l: Argos, The Electra of Euripides
s: Argos is a land, kingdom, and city containing the house of Atreus and the home of Clytemnestra, with Argive people. Associated with Agamemnon, Electra, and Orestes, its mountains hold the action while Aegisthus and Clytemnestra control the royal household. It remembers the golden lamb and is quick to blame. It turns against Orestes; he must win back his fatherland, then flee as Electra departs and Aegisthus is buried there.

l: Troy, The Electra of Euripides
s: is_sacked_by the Greeks [during the Trojan War] Troy is recalled as the city whose war led to Agamemnon’s sacrifice of Iphigenia and whose spoils Clytemnestra distributed to shrines. Castor also says that Helen never set foot in Troy, because a wraith of Helen caused the war and ravishment.

l: the hut, The Electra of Euripides
s: The hut stands on a desolate mountainside near the river Inachus and is the poor home of Electra and the Peasant. It becomes the meeting place where Orestes and Pylades approach Electra and are received by the Peasant.

l: the Chorus, The Electra of Euripides
s: The Chorus is a group of Argive women, maids of Argos, who faithfully support Electra. They visit her at dawn for Hera’s festival and urge joy, but she remains mourning. They recount the golden lamb and Agamemnon’s murder, lament the family’s suffering, celebrate Orestes’s return and Aegisthus’s killing with song and dance, praise Justice, and end with a blessing against mischief.

l: Trojan War, The Electra of Euripides
s: is_a war [led by Agamemnon against Troy] The Trojan War is recalled through Agamemnon's victory over Priam, the burning of Ilion, and the spoils brought back to Argos. Electra remembers Troy and its destruction while condemning the bloodshed and dishonor that followed Agamemnon's return.

l: the murder of Agamemnon, The Electra of Euripides
s: Agamemnon's murder is a betrayal carried out after his return from Troy by Clytemnestra and Aegisthus, who is also described as its instigator and as killing by craft. Clytemnestra defends it as response to Agamemnon's sacrifice of Iphigenia, marital betrayal, and bringing another woman home, but Electra rejects that defense. The killing causes Electra's grief and drives Orestes' planned vengeance: he is urged to kill Aegisthus and Clytemnestra, with Aegisthus's death treated as payment for the blood-debt.

l: Orestes' exile, The Electra of Euripides
s: Orestes' exile is a banishment caused by political danger that separates him from Argos and Electra. As a boy, an old servant takes him from Argos to King Strophios in Phocis to save him from Aegisthus. He wanders with enough bread but suffers humiliation, secretly returns while thought dead, and is then ordered to leave Argos for Athens and later Arcady.

l: Electra's marriage, The Electra of Euripides
s: is_a political safeguard [intended to prevent powerful descendants] Aegisthus arranged Electra's marriage to a poor Peasant so that her children would lack the power to avenge Agamemnon. Although the Peasant is called her husband, Electra says he has never taken her body because he respects her father's greatness.

l: the planned revenge against Clytemnestra and Aegisthus, The Electra of Euripides
s: Orestes, aided by Electra and accompanied by Pylades, undertakes vengeance for Agamemnon’s murder by planning to kill Clytemnestra and Aegisthus. Orestes targets Aegisthus at a feast, while Electra lures Clytemnestra to the house by claiming to have borne a son. They kill both, then face horror, remorse, blood-guilt, and its consequences.

l: Agamemnon's grave, The Electra of Euripides
s: Agamemnon's grave is a desert barrow without customary honors: Electra says it lacks tears, offerings, and myrtle, while Aegisthus insults it drunk. Orestes secretly brings tears, cut hair, and a sacrificed black lamb. Later the Old Man pours wine, lays myrtle, and discovers the ewe and hair, suspecting Orestes' visit.

l: blood vengeance, The Electra of Euripides
s: Blood vengeance is the motive driving Electra and Orestes after Agamemnon's murder. Believing his death demands repayment, they seek divine and ancestral help, target Aegisthus and Clytemnestra, and proceed to kill them; Electra fears Aegisthus may prevent descendants from continuing vengeance.

l: honor and dishonor, The Electra of Euripides
s: is_a social and moral conflict [shaping the treatment of Agamemnon's family] Electra experiences dishonor through poverty, isolation, neglected mourning, and the treatment of Agamemnon's grave. In contrast, the Peasant's restraint and hospitality are presented as honorable, and Orestes observes that true nobility can exist in a poor man.

l: poverty and social rank, The Electra of Euripides
s: is_a social contrast [between the Peasant's poverty and his moral nobility] Electra, though the daughter of a king, lives in a poor hut and performs manual labor, while her husband is a low-status Peasant. Orestes contrasts their poverty with the moral worth of the Peasant and notes that noble birth and wealth do not determine a person's character.

l: Old Man, The Electra of Euripides
s: Old Man, Agamemnon's trusted former servant and Orestes' childhood rescuer and guardian, brings Electra gifts, recognizes Orestes by his brow scar, and confirms him as Agamemnon's son. Knowing Aegisthus' whereabouts, he counsels Orestes to find him and agrees to deceive Clytemnestra about Electra's son.

l: Orestes' recognition, The Electra of Euripides
s: depends_on likeness and recognition signs [especially the scar on Orestes' brow] The Old Man recognizes Orestes after examining him and pointing out the scar on his brow, made when Orestes fell while chasing a fawn with Electra. Electra initially rejects proposed signs involving hair, footprints, and the childhood robe, but accepts the scar as proof and embraces her brother.

l: sacrifice to the wild-wood nymphs, The Electra of Euripides
s: At the pastures, Aegisthus performs worship for the wild-wood nymphs: a wreathed ox is prepared; Orestes and Pylades enter, with no Argive lord present.

l: Electra's house, The Electra of Euripides
s: is_located_in Argos [outside the city and in poverty] Electra's house is the place where she receives the Old Man and Orestes. She intends to draw Clytemnestra to its gate, which she calls the gate leading to herself and Hell.

l: the sword, The Electra of Euripides
s: Electra’s sword, made keen for planned violence, rests across her knees as she waits for news and vows to strike if Orestes dies. It is a weapon used to kill Aegisthus: Orestes takes a heavier sword and strikes him, cleaving his brain and spine.

l: Electra's newborn son, The Electra of Euripides
s: is_presented_as Electra's child [claimed to be ten days old] Electra's newborn son is a deception devised to bring Clytemnestra to the house. Electra tells the Old Man to say that she has been delivered of a male child on the tenth day.

l: likeness and recognition signs, The Electra of Euripides
s: include scar [the decisive sign identifying Orestes] The Old Man first proposes hair, footprints, and the robe from Orestes' childhood as signs of identity. Electra rejects these signs as unreliable or impossible, but the scar on Orestes' brow becomes the decisive proof of recognition.

l: the Gods, The Electra of Euripides
s: The gods are invoked as witnesses to the murders, the family’s inherited suffering, and the judgment to come. Castor says that true judgments flow from the hill in Athens where Orestes will be tried.

l: Justice, The Electra of Euripides
s: Justice is a divine power that ultimately vindicates the wronged, punishing Aegisthus and bringing doom to Clytemnestra for Agamemnon’s murder. Its meaning is contested through claims over Iphigenia and Clytemnestra’s death, then resolved in Athens by equal judges, where mercy prevails.

l: Aegisthus's body, The Electra of Euripides
s: Aegisthus’s corpse is borne into the house of Atreus on a bier; Electra sees and speaks over it, then orders it carried into the hut before Clytemnestra arrives.

l: the battle, The Electra of Euripides
s: is_won_by Orestes [against Aegisthus] The battle is reported as a victory for Orestes, although the messenger's first announcement is understood to concern a broader conflict. Orestes's victory is celebrated with garlands, songs, and cries of joy.

l: the killing of Aegisthus, The Electra of Euripides
s: avenges the murder of Agamemnon [blood against blood] The killing takes place during a sacrifice after Orestes gains Aegisthus's confidence by posing as a traveler. Orestes strikes him while he is bent over the sacrificial omens, and the household thralls recognize Orestes and lower their spears.

l: the house of Atreus, The Electra of Euripides
s: The house of Atreus is a royal house linked to the golden lamb and ancient kingship. Its inherited calamity unfolds through recurring bloodshed among Agamemnon, Aegisthus, Clytemnestra, Electra, and Orestes, whose return restores the old line but leaves matricide threatened.

l: Athena, The Electra of Euripides
s: protects Orestes [from the avenging spirits] Athena is expected to protect Orestes when he clasps her image in her land. Castor says she will hold back the pursuing Spirits with her gorgon shield.

l: Athens, The Electra of Euripides
s: contains Ares' Hill [the place of Orestes' trial] Athens is the place where Orestes must seek refuge at Athena’s image and stand trial for Clytemnestra’s blood. Castor says that its judges will divide equally between death and pardon, allowing Orestes to go free.

l: the House of Tantalus, The Electra of Euripides
s: The Chorus calls Orestes and Electra the seed of Tantalus and says that no family has been as calamitous as theirs. Castor attributes their shared stain to dim forefathers.

l: Keres, The Electra of Euripides
s: Castor refers to the Keres as the deathly forces that came upon the house. He says they were not held back because ancient fate and Apollo’s command required what happened.

l: the sacrifice of Iphigenia, The Electra of Euripides
s: Clytemnestra recalls that Agamemnon deceived Iphigenia with the promise of Achilles’ love, took her to Aulis, and killed her at the altar. She says she could have forgiven the sacrifice if it had saved a city or many children, but not because Helen was wanton.

l: Orestes' trial, The Electra of Euripides
s: establishes justice [by equal judgment and mercy] Orestes is to be tried on the hill in Athens where the great gods once held judgment for a death caused by Ares. Castor says the judges will divide equally between condemning and pardoning him, so that mercy will prevail and he will go free.

l: fate, The Electra of Euripides
s: Castor says that ancient fate and Apollo’s command brought the murders about. Fate is presented as turning like a tide and carrying the family’s inherited stain into the suffering of Orestes and Electra.

l: pollution from blood-guilt, The Electra of Euripides
s: Orestes fears that the blood of his mother makes him impure and that no clean person will share bread with him. The Spirits pursue him as bloodhound-like forces, but Athena is expected to protect him and the trial in Athens will determine his release.

l: The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: The document comprises an introductory note and Euripides’ The Trojan Women, a tragedy centered on the suffering of Troy’s conquered women after the city’s fall. The note calls the play an intense, harrowing witness to misery after conquest, linked in time, though not directly in subject, to Athens’ conquest of Melos. It presents Euripides as opposing strong established power and later leaving amid strife for Macedon, where he wrote the Bacchae and died. The play opens with Poseidon and Pallas Athena agreeing to punish the victorious Greeks for destroying Troy and violating Athena’s holy place: storms and a disastrous return await them. Amid Troy’s ruins, Hecuba mourns Priam, her children, and the city while captive women await enslavement. Talthybius announces the lots: Cassandra goes to Agamemnon, Andromache to Pyrrhus, Polyxena remains at Achilles’ tomb, and Hecuba belongs to Odysseus. Cassandra enters in prophetic frenzy, foretelling Agamemnon’s household’s destruction and Odysseus’s suffering. Andromache arrives with Astyanax, grieving Hector, Polyxena, Troy, and slavery. Talthybius reveals the Greeks’ decree that Astyanax, Hector’s son, must be thrown from the walls lest he become a threat. After soldiers take him, Andromache is sent to the ships. Menelaus then comes for Helen, intending punishment. Helen blames Aphrodite and divine enchantment; Hecuba charges her with freely choosing Paris and causing Troy’s ruin. Menelaus rejects her defense but sends her to Greece alive. Finally, Talthybius returns with Astyanax’s body. Hecuba gives him funeral rites, laying him on Hector’s shield. As the Greeks burn Troy, Hecuba and the other women lament their dead city and depart into slavery.

l: Troaedes, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: Troaedes is an imperfect play, produced in spring of 416 B.C. after the fall and conquest of Melos, with little plot, construction, relief, or variety. Built around conquered women, it intensely studies a great situation after battle, when misery, waiting, and thought remain. Its only dramatic movement gradually extinguishes familiar lights of human life, through four heroic women and less fully characterized female figures. More than art, it is prophecy and bearing of witness, expressing pity for mankind.

l: Euripides, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: Euripides, author of Troaedes, shaped that play around conquered women amid indignant pity and foreboding, lived in deepening strife and hatred, then went to remote Macedon, wrote Bacchae, and died there.

l: Women of Troy, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: Women of Troy are captive Trojan women, the living dramatic focus of the Troaedes, taken as spoils of war and awaiting Greek masters. Called from their huts by Hecuba, they emerge in fear, mourn Troy, and dread separation, enslavement, and unknown Greek destinations. After lots are cast, they are assigned individually to Greek lords and told to follow Cassandra’s bridal cries. They continue lamenting Troy’s destroyed rites, temples, altars, images, festivals, dead, and children, while grieving their forced departure as slaves and wishing Helen never returns to Sparta.

l: Athens, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: Athens, entirely controlled by War Party and bitterly resented by humane minority, conquers Melos; after Melos falls, its fleet prepares for a fatal enterprise against Sicily.

l: Melos, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: is_a neutral Dorian island [before its conquest by Athens] Melos was a neutral Dorian island with a quiet and immemorially ancient town. It was compelled by Athens to take up arms, endured a long siege, and fell in the autumn of 416 B.C.

l: fall and conquest of Melos, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: occurred_in autumn of 416 B.C. The fall and conquest of Melos followed Athens’ long siege of the island after compelling it to take up arms. Melos fell in the autumn of 416 B.C., and the Troaedes was produced in the following spring.

l: massacre and enslavement of Melos, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: is_a great crucial crime of the war [as selected by Thucydides] After conquering Melos, Athens massacred the men and sold the women and children into slavery. The more humane minority bitterly resented this action, and Thucydides selected it as the great crucial crime of the war.

l: Troy, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: Troy is a city and the home of the Trojans, once marked by defensive walls, royal houses, temples, groves, altars, images, sacrifices, festivals, and sacred beauty. Its fate matters most: the Greeks conquer, sack, plunder, and destroy it in war. In the final night, the Greeks' horse enters through its gates, and blood fills its streets and houses. The royal house is destroyed; people are killed or enslaved, with captives kept in Trojan huts and women left mourning. Its treasures are divided, its gods, sanctuaries, temples, and groves are desecrated or lost, and Priam lies unburied. Finally, Greek fire burns the city, its walls collapse, and Troy becomes a smoking, ruined, vanished fallen city whose name and existence pass away.

l: Agamemnon, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: Greek general and king, he chooses Cassandra as bride despite her madness; she prophesies she will kill him and devastate his house.

l: pity, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: Pity is a rebel passion opposing the strong, organized social force, conventional sanctions, and accepted gods. It inspires rebellions, revolutions, martyrdoms, and religions; in the Troaedes it cries out against great wrongs through music, bringing not peace but a sword.

l: the Trojan War, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: The Trojan War is a conflict waged by the Greek army against Troy and its defenders, caused by Helen and described as fought after Paris took Menelaus's bride. Greek assault and conquest bring about Troy's fall. The war ends with the Trojans defeated and the city destroyed and burned; Priam and his sons die, Trojan men are dead, women are divided among Greek masters or enslaved, and children are threatened, including Astyanax's killing. It brings death to armies, separates husbands and wives, deprives children of fathers, and leaves graves far from home.

l: Poseidon, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: Poseidon is a sea god and lord of the Aegean Sea. With Apollo he builds Troy’s walls and protects its ancient people; after Troy’s fall, he joins Pallas Athena’s vengeance, raising storms, reefs, and waves against the returning Greek fleet.

l: Pallas Athena, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: Pallas Athena is a goddess, divine protector and enemy of the Greeks. Though she gives Greeks the means to capture Troy, Ajax's violation of her holy place and Greek inaction drive her to seek vengeance: with Poseidon and Zeus's storms, she brings the fleet a disastrous homecoming.

l: Hecuba, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: Hecuba is the former queen of Troy, wife of Priam, mother of Hector, Paris, Cassandra, and Polyxena, and grandmother of Astyanax. After Troy falls, she is an old, physically weakened captive, allotted as Odysseus's slave. Her story unfolds through grief for her destroyed city, lost royal life, dead family, and the enslavement or loss of those closest to her. She gathers the captive Trojan women and fears their futures; then learns Cassandra, Polyxena, Andromache, and she herself have been assigned to Greek masters or fates. She mourns Priam, her children, Troy, and Astyanax, while urging Andromache to preserve hope through the child. She cannot save him. Hecuba also opposes Helen, urging Menelaus to execute her as punishment for betrayal and Troy's suffering. When Astyanax's body is brought to her, she performs burial rites and laments his violent death. Ordered to leave with Odysseus, she attempts to die in Troy's flames but is restrained, finally departing with the Trojan women toward the Greek ships and slavery.

l: Cassandra, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: Cassandra, Hecuba's daughter, is Apollo's virgin prophetess and priestess, inspired through divine possession. Allotted and forced as captive bride to Agamemnon, she enters carrying a torch and celebrates the marriage in prophetic frenzy. She foretells Agamemnon's death, the destruction of his house, and Odysseus's difficult return, then leaves for the Greek fleet, doomed to die beside Achilles' tomb.

l: Andromache, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: Andromache is a Trojan noblewoman, Hector’s devoted and widowed wife and Astyanax’s mother, renowned as a virtuous wife. After Troy’s fall, the Greeks enslave her; Pyrrhus, Achilles’ son, takes her as captive, prize, and intended concubine, driving her toward Thessaly. Grieving Hector, Polyxena, Troy, her lost life, and Astyanax, she pleads for her son as soldiers take him away, then asks that he receive burial rites rather than be displayed on Hector’s shield.

l: Helen, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: Helen, wife of Menelaus and queen of Sparta, is carried by Paris from Sparta to Troy. Her beauty and relationship with Paris are treated as sources of power, disgrace, and the conflict that brings the Greek expedition and Troy's fall. After Troy's defeat, she is a captive and prize among Trojan prisoners. Hecuba and Menelaus accuse her of guilt and of causing the war, while Helen pleads that Aphrodite compelled her, that she tried to escape, and that she was taken by force. Menelaus rejects her defense and sends her under Greek escort toward the ships and Argos.

l: Talthybius, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: Talthybius is a Greek herald and agent of the Greek army who serves Agamemnon. He conveys the Greeks’ decisions after the lots assign Cassandra to Agamemnon, Hecuba to Odysseus, and Andromache to Pyrrhus, escorting Cassandra toward the fleet. Reluctantly bearing bad news, he reports the council’s order for Astyanax’s death, takes the child from Andromache, and later delivers his body to Hecuba, cleanses his wounds, and prepares his grave. At the end, he orders the Greek captains to burn Troy and has Hecuba taken away.

l: Menelaus, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: Menelaus is a Greek king of Sparta and commander of Greek soldiers and ships, still regarded as Helen’s husband. He seeks to take Helen to Greece for punishment, rejecting enchantment as an excuse and enforcing marital faithfulness. Entering richly armed, he hears Helen and Hecuba, postpones execution, and orders Helen sent by ship, threatening punishment in Argos.

l: Hector, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: Hector is a Trojan prince of Troy, husband of Andromache and father of Astyanax. Remembered as Troy's mighty defender and a warrior with thousands beside him, his valor leaves Astyanax feared after Hector's death. His battle-worn shield, marked by his handgrip and sweat, becomes Astyanax's burial bier.

l: Paris, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: Paris is a Trojan prince, dead son of Hecuba, and a beautiful man. Beneath Mount Ida’s trees he judged three goddesses. His love for Helen causes Troy’s destruction: Menelaus says he stole his bride, while Helen calls him Alexander, Breaker-down-of-Men, and says Aphrodite accompanied him.

l: Polyxena, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: Polyxena is a Trojan, daughter of Priam and Hecuba, and a Trojan princess made a sacrificial victim. She is set apart to watch Achilles' tomb, then is killed across it as an offering to the dead; Andromache calls her death sweeter than misery.

l: Greeks, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: Greeks are a conquering army that captures and destroys Troy after entering through the wooden Trojan Horse. They win the Trojan War but enact its harsh costs: killing people, violating sacred places, burning the city, and enslaving and dividing surviving Trojan women among their leaders. They award Helen to Menelaus, enslave Andromache, and order Astyanax thrown from Ilion’s tower because they fear he could restore Troy; they may deny him burial. As they prepare to sail home, Cassandra describes their victory as marked by dead soldiers, bereaved women, absent children, and graves, while Pallas Athena and Poseidon plan to make their homecoming disastrous.

l: Trojans, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: The Trojans are defeated by the Greeks in the war for Troy. Their city, sanctuaries, families, children, kings, and freedom are destroyed or lost during the sack. The dead and ruined city remain behind, while the surviving Trojan women are treated as spoils of war, await enslavement, and are carried away as captives to bear the children of the foe.

l: Greek army, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: The Greek army fights at Troy for ten years in a war that leaves no man's land moved. It is associated with deciding the women's destinations by lot, accompanies Menelaus, drags Helen from her chamber, and escorts her toward the shore.

l: Argos, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: Cassandra is assigned to go to Argos as Agamemnon's bride. She calls herself a bride going to the king's bed there. Argos is the place to which Menelaus intends to take Helen after the voyage. He says that a severe punishment awaiting her there will serve as a lasting warning to women about faithfulness.

l: Troy's walls, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: are_burning fire [as the city is destroyed] Troy's ruins are filled with fire, smoke, and the forms of the Greeks burning the city. The walls and towers collapse in a great crash until the ruins disappear into smoke and darkness.

l: Greek fleet, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: The Greek fleet is a group of ships on Troy’s shore, prepared to carry Greeks, Helen, Cassandra, and other Trojan captives away toward home. As departure nears, it becomes the destination for captives and Helen is assigned another ship; after it sails, Poseidon intends to assail it with storms and waves.

l: Trojan Horse, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: Trojan Horse is a towering wooden offering to Pallas, marvelous and gold outside but dark steel within. Made by Epeios through Pallas Athena's mysteries, it conceals Greek soldiers. After the Greeks withdraw, Trojans bring it through Troy's gates as a victory offering; its armed occupants destroy the city.

l: fall of Troy, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: The fall of Troy is the Greek conquest of the city, attributed to the Greek attack and the wooden horse that passed through its walls. It brings the killing of Priam, the deaths of Troy's men and Paris, blood in the sanctuaries, the destruction of the citadel, and the collapse of walls and towers. Greek forces carry Troy's wealth to their ships, while fire, desolation, and scorn consume the city. The conquest most grievously determines the survivors' fate: Trojan women, including Andromache and Hecuba, are allotted to Greek masters and taken away as captives; Astyanax is killed because the Greeks fear Hector's lineage. Though Hecuba imagines rebuilding, the final departure for the Greek ships leaves Troy destroyed, without defenders or a future.

l: enslavement of the Trojan women, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: The enslavement of the Trojan women is a captivity imposed after Troy’s defeat in the Trojan War. Captured women are allotted to Greek leaders and territories, facing forced lives as bondmaids, household workers, water carriers, nurses, or unwilling bedmates. Hecuba is assigned to Odysseus, while Andromache is chosen for Achilles’ son’s household and fears both betraying Hector and provoking further suffering. The women mourn Troy, are ordered from their ruined land, and depart toward Greek ships and bondage.

l: Greek homecoming, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: is_endangered_by storm sent against the Greek fleet [through divine vengeance] The Greeks are waiting for favorable wind so they can return home to their wives and children. Pallas Athena asks that their homecoming never reach a home, and Poseidon agrees to obstruct it after the final ship leaves.

l: storm sent against the Greek fleet, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: Pallas Athena asks Zeus for rain, hail, darkness, and lightning, while Poseidon promises to make the sea roads wild. The storm is intended to drown Greek soldiers and ships near Euboea and among the surrounding reefs and islands.

l: Greek siege of Troy, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: The Greek forces came by sea and attacked Troy with spears before entering through the wooden horse. The siege ended in the destruction of the city and the enslavement of its surviving women.

l: slavery and captivity, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: Slavery and captivity are the imposed fate of the defeated Trojan women: confined near ruined Troy, separated from their city, and awaiting lots assigning Greek masters and destinations. It unfolds from confinement and uncertainty to Hecuba’s expectation of humiliating servile labor.

l: grief and lamentation, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: Grief and lamentation are expressed by Andromache, Hecuba, and captive women through cries, songs, tears, and memories. They mourn Troy’s ruin, Priam, children, families, lost homes and status, and the dead. Their mourning deepens into despair as the living are carried from happiness into misery, making death seem sweeter than hopeless life.

l: divine vengeance, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: Pallas Athena and Poseidon unite in vengeance against the Greeks for Ajax's offense and the Greeks' destruction of sacred places. Their planned punishment is the ruin of the Greek fleet and a deadly, unsuccessful return voyage.

l: Odysseus, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: Odysseus is the king of Ithaca who receives and owns Hecuba as an allotted captive slave. At the Greek council he prevails in deciding to kill Astyanax. Afterward, Cassandra foretells that his homeward journey will bring ten years of suffering, leaving him lost and unfriended.

l: Achilles' tomb, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: is_watched_by Polyxena [according to the allotment] Polyxena is said to rest apart at Achilles' tomb. The tomb is presented as the place where she is being kept after the lots are cast.

l: torches, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: Torches appear when Cassandra enters, carrying a great torch and singing as if for a wedding. Hecuba takes Cassandra's torch and orders it carried back, while Cassandra later tears off her wreaths and leaves.

l: Cassandra's prophecy, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: Cassandra's prophecy declares that she will kill Agamemnon and destroy his house. It also foretells Odysseus's long, lonely suffering and presents the Greeks' apparent victory as a source of future grief.

l: lot-casting, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: determines the Trojan women's destinations [after the fall of Troy] Talthybius announces that the lots have been cast to determine the women's destinations. The lots separate them among Agamemnon, Pyrrhus, Odysseus, and the place where Polyxena is kept.

l: Cassandra's forced marriage, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: Cassandra is assigned to Agamemnon as a bride, despite her sacred status as Apollo's chosen priestess and her lack of consent. She treats the marriage as a wedding while foretelling that it will bring death to Agamemnon's house.

l: Polyxena's death, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: is_a human sacrifice [at Achilles' tomb] The text says that Polyxena rests apart to watch Achilles' tomb, but it does not directly describe her death in this unit.

l: sack of Troy, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: The sack of Troy includes Priam's murder at the altar, the destruction of the citadel, the killing of men in the streets and houses, and the capture of the women. The chorus remembers the city changing from celebration to bloodshed and desolation.

l: marriage, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: is_a source of grief [for the Trojan captives] Marriage is presented through Cassandra's forced assignment to Agamemnon and her wedding songs with torches and hymns. Her apparent bridal celebration is linked to death, vengeance, and the destruction of Agamemnon's house.

l: war and its cost, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: The text emphasizes that war costs soldiers their lives, wives their husbands, children their fathers, and the dead their familiar burial places. Cassandra says Troy gained glory by dying for its people, while the Greeks gained grief, isolation, and a hollow victory.

l: Astyanax, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: Astyanax is Hector’s son, a child and prince of Troy. Carried by Andromache, he is condemned by the Greek army because they fear he may restore Troy. A soldier takes him to Troy’s wall, where Greeks hurl him from Ilion’s tower. Dead before knowing life and love, he is mourned by Hecuba, wrapped in garments, and buried on Hector’s shield, with a grave.

l: Astyanax's death, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: Astyanax's death is a Greek-ordered child killing. On Odysseus's advice, the Greek army fears Hector's son may restore his fallen land and become a threat. Soldiers take him from Andromache, who cannot save him, to dash him from Troy's wall. Hecuba condemns the murder as shameful and mourns his lost youth and greatness.

l: love, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: causes the fall of Troy [Paris's destructive love] Love is presented as a force that helped bring Troy honor and greatness but also contributed to its destruction through Paris's love for Helen. Andromache's love for Hector remains loyal after his death and makes the prospect of another man's embrace unbearable.

l: fate and divine destruction, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: overcome Hecuba [in her many sorrows] Fate and divine power are described as overwhelming Troy and reducing the mighty to helplessness. Hecuba says that God's great wave has conquered her, while the Chorus recalls divine destruction falling twice upon the Dardanian walls and blames divine and destructive forces for Troy's ruin.

l: the three goddesses' judgment, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: Paris judges gifts from Pallas, Hera, and Cypris: military victory, royal dominion, and Helen’s love. He chooses Cypris as fairest for Helen’s love, a judgment Helen says led to her being taken from Sparta.

l: Helen's beauty, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: is_a birthright [regarded by Helen as both potential glory and stigma] Helen's beauty is described as a power that can ensnare strong men, destroy cities, and bring fire upon houses. Helen calls it a birthright that has become a mark of slavery, while Hecuba treats it as part of Helen's dangerous appeal and pride.

l: Helen's alleged enchantment, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: is_attributed_to Aphrodite [by Helen's defense] Helen claims that Cypris or Aphrodite enchanted her and caused her to forget her home and follow Paris. Hecuba denies that goddesses compelled Helen, arguing instead that Helen's own desire for Paris, wealth, and honor led her away.

l: Helen's guilt and innocence, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: Helen presents herself as wronged and innocent, saying that divine power caused her departure and that she tried to escape Troy. Hecuba and Menelaus reject this defense, asserting that Helen willingly chose Paris and bears responsibility for the war and its dead.

l: justice and punishment, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: requires marital faithfulness [as a law for women] Hecuba calls for Helen's death as justice for the destruction and deaths caused by her betrayal. Menelaus initially speaks of killing her but instead sends her toward Greece, where he promises a severe and exemplary punishment.

l: marital faithfulness, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: is_violated_by Helen [in Hecuba's accusation] Hecuba presents Helen's departure from Menelaus as the betrayal of a husband's bed and says that a woman who betrays her husband should be judged and die. Menelaus says Helen's punishment will bind the law of faithfulness upon women.

l: the Trojan captives' exile, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: The Trojan women are forcibly taken from Troy by sea to Greece as Greek slaves, mourning captivity and separation from their children, husbands, city, sacred places, and homeland as the ships depart.

l: Helen's execution, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: is_intended_by Menelaus [as a future punishment in Argos] Helen expects that Menelaus may execute her, and Hecuba repeatedly urges him to kill her. Menelaus does not execute her in this unit; instead, he orders her escorted to the shore and threatens a later punishment in Argos.

l: the sea voyage to Greece, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: After Troy’s fall, Helen is sent by ship toward Greece under Menelaus’s orders, while Trojan captive women are carried toward Argos and Greek lands, mourning exile as galleys depart the ruined city.

l: Trojan women, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: are_enslaved Greeks [after Troy's destruction] The Trojan women mourn Astyanax, help provide garments and funeral offerings, and carry his body out on Hector's shield. They are ordered to leave when the Greek trumpet sounds and are taken toward the ships and slavery.

l: Hector's shield, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: Hector's bronze-fronted, battle-worn war shield, once feared in battle, bears his hand and sweat, protects Astyanax as a burial covering, and carries the child to the grave.

l: fire, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: destroys Troy [burning the city from its heart] The Greeks fling fire into Troy's heart and ignite the ruined city. The flames rise through the dusk, consume the houses and walls, and send smoke across the sky as Troy disappears.

l: divine fate, The Trojan Women of Euripides
s: governs Troy [bringing its greatness low] Hecuba says that God has turned Troy in His hand, thrust its high things low, and shaken its hills like dust. She concludes that prayers, incense, and sacrifices did not prevent the city's destruction, and the women lament that the divine father of the Phrygians sees their suffering but is pitiless.

l: Iphigenia in Tauris
s: Euripides’ Iphigenia in Tauris is presented as a romantic play of threatened human sacrifice, exile, deception, recognition, and release rather than a true tragedy. Iphigenia, Agamemnon’s eldest daughter, tells how Artemis saved her from sacrifice at Aulis and made her priestess among the Tauri, whose custom is to kill foreign strangers at the goddess’s altar. Haunted by homesickness and grief, she dreams that her brother Orestes has died and makes funeral offerings for him. Orestes, pursued by Furies after killing Clytemnestra, arrives from Argos with Pylades under Apollo’s command to take Artemis’s divine image to Greece. After Orestes suffers madness and fights the Taurians, the two men are captured. Iphigenia questions them, learning of Troy’s fall, Agamemnon’s and Clytemnestra’s deaths, and Orestes’s misery. She proposes saving Pylades to carry a tablet and message to Argos, while Orestes accepts death. As she dictates the message, he recognizes her as his supposedly dead sister; they prove their identities through family memories and rejoice, though they remain endangered. Iphigenia then plans their escape. She tells King Thoas that Orestes, Pylades, and the image need purification at the sea, and the captive Greek women promise silence. She leads the men and image away, frees Orestes, and reaches a Greek ship. When Thoas orders pursuit, Athena intervenes: Orestes must bring Iphigenia and the image to Greece. The image is assigned a temple at Halae, Iphigenia an office at Brauron, and Thoas frees the women and permits the Greeks to depart.

l: Iphigenia in Tauris, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: Iphigenia in Tauris is a romantic play set in Tauris, based on a human-sacrifice rite. Beginning in a tragic atmosphere of exile and sadness, it moves through peril, reflection, recognition, and Iphigenia and Orestes's escape to a happy ending.

l: Greek tragedy, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: has_nucleus Aition [a cause or origin] Greek tragedies are said to have an Aition, or cause or origin, that explains a ritual, observance, or great event. Their frequent basis in Tomb Rituals helps explain the shadow of death and the sense of fatality associated with them.

l: Aition, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: explains ritual [or an observance or great event] An Aition is a cause or origin underlying a Greek tragedy, usually connected with a ritual, observance, or great event. The Iphigenia in Tauris is based on a sacred rite in which a victim is brought close to death but does not die.

l: Tomb Ritual, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: is_a Aition [the usual sacred basis of tragedy] Tomb Rituals serve as the nucleus of many Greek tragedies and commemorate a hero’s funeral or grave. Their presence makes death seem inevitable because the ritual presupposes that the hero must die.

l: Halae, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: Halae, an Attic boundary place near Karystus’ Rock, receives Athena’s commanded temple for Artemis’ image and holds Artemis Tauropolos’ festival: a human victim reaches the altar, is sword-touched at the throat, then released.

l: Artemis Tauropolos, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: has_altar Halae [in Attica] Artemis Tauropolos was worshipped at Halae in a rite involving the symbolic near-sacrifice and release of a human victim. The preface connects this rite with what happened to Orestes among the Tauri and to Iphigenia at Aulis.

l: Artemis, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: Artemis is a virgin goddess, child of Leto and twin sibling of Apollo, worshipped at Tauris as a huntress and associated with a heaven-sent sacred image. At Aulis she saves Iphigenia from sacrifice by substituting a fawn, carrying her to Tauris, and making her priestess. In Tauris her sanctuary and altar receive rites involving the blood of strangers, leading Iphigenia to accuse her of cruelty. Artemis possesses the divine image kept in the Taurian shrine; Apollo commands Orestes to remove it, and Iphigenia says it must be purified. The image is ultimately taken to Greece and honored at Halae as Artemis Tauropole.

l: Iphigenia, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: Iphigenia is the eldest daughter of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra, sister of Orestes and Electra, and a Greek woman from Argos. Thought dead after a supposed sacrifice at Aulis, she was saved by Artemis through substitution by a fawn and taken to Tauris. There, unwillingly serving as Artemis’ priestess, she consecrates captured strangers before they are slain. Exile, homesickness, and bitterness toward those connected to her supposed murder shape her life, while she rejects the Taurian human-sacrifice custom as unworthy of divine goodness. After a prophetic dream makes her believe Orestes dead, she performs his funeral rite. When Orestes and Pylades are captured, she questions Orestes about Greece and her family, seeks to send a tablet to Argos, reveals herself as Iphigenia believed dead, and recognizes him as her surviving brother. Reunited, she learns Electra lives and is married to Pylades, but fears the rite will still kill Orestes. Determined to save the Greek strangers, she devises a false purification for Orestes and Pylades, persuades King Thoas to allow it, leads them from the temple, frees Orestes, and carries Artemis’ image to their ship. Athena then assigns her to Brauron, where she is to serve, live, die, and be buried.

l: Orestes, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: Orestes is a Greek, the first brought to the Taurian altar, and the firstborn son of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra, brother of Iphigenia and Electra, native to Mycenae and an exile from Argolis. He kills Clytemnestra to avenge Agamemnon, but is cursed, pursued by Furies, and driven into madness. Though tried at the Ares' Hill tribunal and acquitted by Athena, he remains afflicted by some Furies and seeks freedom. Apollo commands him to travel with his sworn companion and follower Pylades to Tauris, seize Artemis's image, and carry it to Attic soil or Greece. In Tauris, mental torment leads him to fight the herds; he and Pylades are captured and brought bound to Artemis's temple for execution. Facing death, he shows leadership and refuses to abandon Iphigenia. When she dictates a message, the long-separated siblings recognize one another through shared memories. They join an escape plan, flee Tauris with Artemis's image, and Athena protects them from Thoas and directs the image's journey to Greece, where human sacrifice will no longer stain it.

l: the Tauri, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: The Tauri are a savage people who possess Artemis’s heaven-fallen image and sacrifice strangers reaching their shores, actions contrasted with Orestes and Pylades’s bravery and unselfishness.

l: Tauris, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: Tauris is a remote, desolate, savage country beyond the Symplegades, ruled by King Thoas. It is the land of the Tauri, whose custom is to slaughter foreign captives for Artemis at her temple and altar, where Artemis has placed Iphigenia as priestess. Iphigenia lives there as Orestes and Pylades are held for execution, but hopes to send Pylades away. In the end, Orestes, Iphigenia, and Artemis’s image escape; Thoas pursues them, then accepts Athena’s decision that they must leave.

l: image of Artemis, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: The image of Artemis, believed to have fallen from heaven, stands in the Taurian shrine and is associated with the sacrifice of strangers. Apollo commands Orestes to seize it and carry it to Attic earth for freedom, so it will no longer be stained with human sacrifice. Iphigenia removes it during a false cleansing, claiming it is defiled, takes it aboard the Greek ship, and Athena orders its installation at Halae.

l: Tauric rite of Artemis, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: The Tauric rite of Artemis is a sacrificial ritual for foreign strangers, especially Greeks brought to the sanctuary. Captives such as Orestes and Pylades are sent to Iphigenia, who performs preliminary acts with the blood-bowl and holy spray. At the altar, victims are purified with water, struck by attendants, touched on the throat with a sword, and released; the rite also sends them toward a rocky gulf and holy fire.

l: the sacrifice of Iphigenia at Aulis, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: The sacrifice of Iphigenia at Aulis is a human-sacrifice ritual ordered by Artemis to end the Greek fleet’s immobility during the Trojan expedition. Calchas declares that Agamemnon must sacrifice his daughter, whom Agamemnon promises to Artemis and brings to Aulis by falsely claiming she will marry Achilles. At the altar, she is believed to be killed by her father. At the last moment, however, Artemis prevents the sacrifice, removes Iphigenia, and substitutes a deer or fawn, leaving Agamemnon believing his sword struck her.

l: Agamemnon, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: Agamemnon, son of Atreus, is king of Argos and of the Argive royal house, husband of Clytemnestra, and father of Iphigenia and Orestes. Unable to sail from Aulis against Troy, he leads the Trojan expedition for Menelaus and Helen and joins Odysseus in summoning Iphigenia with a false marriage promise. He supposedly sacrifices her to Artemis. Later he is reported dead, killed when Clytemnestra stabs him; his death devastates Orestes.

l: Clytemnestra, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: Clytemnestra, mother of Iphigenia and Orestes and wife of Agamemnon, murders Agamemnon by stabbing him; Orestes later kills her in vengeance for Agamemnon’s death.

l: Aulis, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: Aulis is the site where Agamemnon gathers the Greek fleet for Troy, but weather holds it there. He vows Iphigenia to Artemis and attempts to sacrifice her; she is believed slain, yet Artemis rescues her before the sacrifice is completed. Later, messages and Orestes recall Aulis as the place of her supposed death.

l: Apollo, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: Apollo, child of Leto and brother of Artemis, kills Snake at Pytho and rules its oracle. He commands and sends Orestes to carry Artemis’s image from Tauris to Attica, establishing the mission, freedom, divine intent, and Orestes’s contact with Iphigenia.

l: Euripides, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: Euripides wrote Iphigenia in Tauris, a subtle, mobile, poignant romantic play whose recognition scene modeled Aristotle, and Iphigenia in Aulis, probably unfinished at his death.

l: Greece, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: Greece is a homeland and desired destination: Iphigenia was taken from it and longs to return, while Orestes recounts Greek leaders’ suffering after Troy. It becomes the goal of Orestes, Pylades, Iphigenia, Greek women, and Artemis’s image; Athena orders the image established there and the freed women returned home.

l: Greeks, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: The Greeks prepare to sail against Troy, linked in Iphigenia’s memory to betrayal and violence at Aulis. When Greek strangers reach Tauris, she pities and aids them. They free Orestes and Iphigenia, carry Artemis’s image toward Greece, and are saved from a squall by Athena.

l: Iphigenia myth, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: has_forms varying forms [like the great Greek legends] The Iphigenia myths take many forms and are described as conjectural reconstructions of supposed early history. They combine traditions about Iphigenia, Artemis, sacrifice, redemption, the Tauri, and the movement of Artemis’s worship into Attica.

l: Iphigenia and Orestes's escape, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: Iphigenia and Orestes’s escape is the joint flight from Tauris to Greece after Iphigenia recognizes Orestes and abandons her earlier plan to save only Pylades. To avoid the Taurian sacrifice, Iphigenia, Orestes, Pylades, and the Greek women deceive King Thoas with a false purification, secretly take Artemis’s image to a ship, and seek passage to Argos. Tauric forces and a storm nearly prevent them, but Athena intervenes and secures their departure.

l: Pylades, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: Pylades is a man, Prince of Phocis, son of King Strophios, Electra’s husband, and Orestes’ cousin, closest friend, devoted follower, and sworn companion. He accompanies Orestes from the mission to take Artemis’s image from Tauris through their attempted escape, sharing Orestes’ plan, madness, affliction, and guilt. Though Orestes is chief, Pylades is brave, unselfish, protective, and steadfast: he tends and shields Orestes during madness and attack, refuses to abandon him when they are bound, and is willing to die with him rather than return in shame. As bearer of Iphigenia’s tablet, he swears to carry her message to Argos, helps reveal Orestes’ identity, and urges Orestes to seize freedom.

l: Thoas, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: Thoas is the king of Tauris who rules the Taurians and insists on slaughtering strangers, though he is described as a fine fellow. He questions Iphigenia, accepts her claim that strangers and the image have been defiled, and orders confinement, guards, restrictions, and cleansing. After Iphigenia and Orestes escape with the image, he orders pursuit, then obeys Athena, releases the women, halts the galleys, and wishes them well.

l: Women of the Chorus, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: Women of the Chorus are Greek women in captivity, exiled from their heart’s home among savage people and cruel gods. Their sea- and water-filled lyrics express longing for Hellas. As Iphigenia’s comrades, they promise Zeus to keep her planned escape secret and aid Iphigenia, Orestes, and Pylades. Accused by Thoas, they are declared faithful by Athena, praise the escape, and depart peacefully.

l: romantic play, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: A romantic play is described as moving through ingenuity, make-believe, perils, escapes, and often a happy ending. It may be artistically different from tragedy because its atmosphere is less consistently sincere, although happiness is not considered less beautiful than grief.

l: exile and homesickness, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: Exile and homesickness provide the central shadow over Iphigenia in Tauris instead of the shadow of death. Iphigenia, Orestes, and the Women of the Chorus are all separated from their heart’s home and long for Hellas beyond the sea.

l: Argos, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: Argos is the ancestral homeland of Orestes and Iphigenia, remembered as a royal home of city and rituals. Separated from it, Iphigenia longs to return and hopes to send a message there, believing Orestes has died. Orestes, exiled while their uncle rules Argos, hopes to return, asks for a burial there if he dies, and promises to bring Iphigenia home across the sea.

l: the Furies, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: pursue Orestes [as blood-avengers] The Furies pursue Orestes because of the bloodshed in his family. Some accept the judgment at Athens and settle beneath that place, but others continue to cling to him like bloodhounds.

l: messenger, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: The Messenger tells Thoas that the strangers have escaped and that Iphigenia stole the image of Artemis. He recounts the false cleansing, the fight at the shore, the ship’s struggle against the sea, and his return to summon Thoas.

l: Chorus of Captive Greek Women, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: The Chorus of Captive Greek Women is a group of Greek handmaids enslaved at Tauris and assigned to Iphigenia. Formerly from Hellas, they serve as witnesses and commentators, mourning the house of Atreus, recalling Orestes and Pylades’ voyage, and longing for Greece and freedom. When Orestes and Pylades are brought bound for slaughter, they pity them yet rejoice at a captive’s possible return.

l: Athena, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: Athena, a goddess and daughter of Zeus, appears to halt Thoas’s pursuit of Orestes and Iphigenia, directs Artemis’s image to Halae and Iphigenia to Brauron, establishes a blood rite, and makes equal life-and-death votes favor mercy.

l: the play, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: is_first_performed first performance of the play [between the years 414 and 412 B.C.] The play includes Iphigenia, Orestes, Pylades, Thoas, a Herdsman, a Messenger, a Chorus of Captive Greek Women, and the Goddess Pallas Athena. It was first performed between the years 414 and 412 B.C.

l: Agamemnon's murder, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: The murder of Agamemnon was committed by Clytemnestra. Agamemnon's murder is attributed to his wife, who stabbed him after his return. Orestes later killed the murderer in an act he regarded as justice for his father's death.

l: killing of Clytemnestra by Orestes, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: Orestes, acting amid his father’s wrongs and with Pylades, kills Clytemnestra; the bloodguilt brings Furies’ pursuit and leads Iphigenia to require purification.

l: the gods, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: The gods are described by Orestes as no clearer than dreams, with their ways full of turmoil. He blames a prophetic divine power for leading him to kill his mother and then abandoning him to die in Tauris.

l: the temple, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: The temple is a sanctuary on a barbaric, desolate sea-coast, housing Artemis’s divine image in a sacred shrine and an altar stained with sacrificial blood and the spoils of slain men. Iphigenia serves there as priestess. Orestes and Pylades arrive to steal the image, are freed under its holy rule, and preparations are made within. It becomes the site of a supposed purification as Iphigenia leads the strangers and image toward the sea, while Thoas attempts to answer their escape; Athena orders a new temple at Halae for the image.

l: the sea, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: purifies the purification ritual [by its salt spray] The sea is presented as the place where impurity can be washed away. Iphigenia uses that belief to persuade Thoas that the strangers and the image must be carried to a secluded channel near the ship.

l: the altar, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: is_used_for the sacrifice of Iphigenia [at Aulis] The altar in the sanctuary is stained with the blood of sacrificed strangers, and the spoils of slain men hang nearby. Iphigenia is expected to prepare the captured Greeks for sacrifice upon it.

l: the ship, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: The ship carries Orestes and Pylades from Argolis to Tauris, then waits moored near a purification channel with fifty oars ready. It later carries Orestes, Iphigenia, and Artemis’s image toward Greece, struggles against current and squall toward rocks, and is saved when Athena has Poseidon calm the waves.

l: Orestes' matricide, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: is_committed_by Orestes [in vengeance for Agamemnon] Orestes says that he killed his mother in order to avenge his father at the command of a god. He has since wandered through Hellas, pursued by shapes of pain and tormented by visions of Furies.

l: the planned theft of Artemis' image, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: The planned theft of Artemis' image is Apollo's prescribed means to release Orestes from suffering. Orestes and Pylades intend to wait for night and secretly take it, fearing death if seen, but are captured. Iphigenia instead plans and carries out its removal under cover of a purification rite.

l: Iphigenia's dream, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: Iphigenia dreams her father’s house collapses, leaving a human-haired, speaking oaken pillar; she takes the pillar and cleansing drops poured over it as signs of Orestes’ death.

l: Orestes' madness, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: Orestes's madness began after the bloodshed he refuses to name and led him through exile and suffering. Although judgment at Athens freed him from death, some of the Furies still pursue him, and he hopes that completing Apollo's command will end his madness.

l: Mycenae, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: is_the_home_of Orestes [formerly rich land] Mycenae is named as Orestes' home and as the place associated with the family whose fate Iphigenia anxiously investigates.

l: the Argive royal house, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: The Argive royal house, ruled by king Agamemnon, is stricken by his murder and ensuing familial bloodshed, bringing deaths and suffering to Agamemnon, Clytemnestra, and Orestes; Electra remains alive and unmarried.

l: the tablet, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: contains the message to Orestes [written by Iphigenia] The tablet contains Iphigenia's written message and is entrusted to Pylades for delivery to Argos. Iphigenia also repeats its contents aloud so that the message will survive even if the tablet is lost at sea.

l: the message to Orestes, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: identifies Iphigenia [as alive in Tauris] The message identifies its sender as Iphigenia, who was believed to have been slain at Aulis but is still alive in Tauris. It asks Orestes to take her back to Argos and explains that Artemis saved her by substituting a fawn at the sacrifice.

l: the oath, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: binds Pylades [to deliver the tablet or its contents] Pylades swears to carry Iphigenia's tablet to the friend she names, invoking Zeus as witness. Iphigenia promises to send him safely from Tauris and swears that her foot will never tread Greek earth again if she fails.

l: the Trojan War, Iphigenia in Tauris
s: The Trojan War is recalled through the fall of Troy and the return of the Greek armies. Iphigenia asks Orestes about Helen, Calchas, Odysseus, Achilles, and the Greek leaders connected with the war.
